lesson.text: Most people hear "collect less" and reach for the delete key. But the sharper question is not how much data you hold — it is what SHAPE it is in. A record naming a sick villager, and a count of how many were sick, can answer the same question — only one of them can ruin a life if it leaks. Shaping the data means transforming it so the risk falls away while the answer survives.

THE EARLIER, THE SAFER — Transform data as early in the pipeline as possible. If identifiers are stripped at the source, every system downstream — every vault, backup, report and recipient — never holds the dangerous version at all. You cannot leak what you never stored. Deleting downstream is cleanup; transforming upstream is design. (This is data protection BY DESIGN and BY DEFAULT.)
AGGREGATION — report the statistic, drop the individuals. "34 cases of fever" instead of thirty-four named patients.
GENERALISATION — replace precise values with ranges. An exact age becomes "30–40"; a street becomes a district.
SUPPRESSION — remove the field entirely where nothing else will do.
PSEUDONYMISATION — swap identifiers for codes. Useful, but reversible: still personal data, not a finish line.

PRIVATE AND USELESS IS ALSO A FAILURE — Strip too hard and a report can end up saying only "something happened, somewhere" — technically safe, and useless to whoever asked for it. Anonymisation must still SERVE THE PURPOSE. The test is not "how little can I reveal?" but "what is the least that still answers the question?" Too much detail is a breach waiting to happen; too little is a decision no one can make. Proportion, again.

Before designing any flow, ask three things in order: (1) What decision does the recipient need to make? (2) What is the smallest shape of data that supports that decision? (3) Where in the pipeline can I put it in that shape — earliest wins. Answer those and minimisation stops being a rule you comply with and becomes an architecture you design.

quiz.q: The Council needs to plan the winter medicine budget. What is the SMALLEST shape of data that answers their question?
choices: A total number of sick villagers
explain: Wrong — far more than the decision requires. Names add risk with no added value to a budget question.
Correct — enough to plan medicine by illness, and no more. This is the smallest shape that still answers the question.
Wrong — private, but useless. A single total can't tell them which medicines to buy.
quiz.hint: Ask what decision they must make, then give exactly that much.

variant.q: A guild wants to know which MONTH illness peaks, to time their supply run. Smallest useful shape?
explain: Wrong — far more than the decision requires. Named daily logs add risk with no added value to a timing question.
Correct — enough to see which month peaks, and no more. This is the smallest shape that still answers the question.
Wrong — private, but useless. A yearly total can't reveal which month to prepare for.

quiz.q: Why is transforming data EARLY in the pipeline better than deleting it later?
choices: Downstream systems never hold the risky version
explain: Wrong — speed is irrelevant to the privacy argument here.
Correct — you cannot leak what a system never stored. Every vault, backup, and report downstream stays clean by construction.
Wrong — no such rule exists. The principle is by-design, not by-deadline.
quiz.hint: What can a vault leak if the dangerous version never reached it?

variant.q: A pipeline runs Collection → Processing → Storage → Report. Where should identifiers be stripped?
explain: Wrong — Storage would already hold the risky version by then, along with anything backed up from it.
Correct — the earliest point after collection. Strip there and nothing downstream ever holds the dangerous version at all.
Wrong — by the time a report is read, every earlier stage has already stored the risky version.

quiz.q: A report replaces exact ages with ranges and removes street names. Which techniques are these?
explain: Wrong — aggregation would report a statistic instead of a person; pseudonymisation would swap in a code, not a range.
Correct — an age blurred into a band is generalisation; a field removed outright is suppression.
Wrong — neither technique here locks or restricts the data; both reshape the values themselves.
quiz.hint: One blurs a value into a band; the other removes a field outright.

quiz.q: Which change makes data ANONYMOUS rather than merely pseudonymous?
choices: Replacing names with codes held in a key
Publishing only group counts with no way back to individuals
explain: Wrong — reversible wherever the key exists. Pseudonymized data remains personal data under the law.
Correct — with no route back to any individual, no one, using reasonable means, can re-identify. That's the bar anonymization has to clear.
Wrong — also reversible with the key. Encryption protects the data; it doesn't anonymise it.
quiz.hint: If someone, somewhere, holds the way back — is it truly anonymous?

variant.q: A dataset replaces every villager's name with a random token, and the clerk keeps the token list in her drawer. Anonymous?
choices: No — the drawer is the way back
explain: Wrong — a token is only ever pseudonymous while something, somewhere, can reverse it.
Correct — the drawer is the key. As long as it exists, this is pseudonymization, not anonymization.

quiz.q: A guild asks for health data to decide where to dig a well. You aggregate so hard that the output says only "people are ill somewhere in the village." What have you done wrong?
choices: Nothing — maximum privacy is always correct
Over-stripped: the data no longer serves its purpose
explain: Wrong — privacy that prevents the decision it was collected for isn't a win, it's a different failure.
Correct — private and useless is still a failure. The shape has to survive carrying the answer, not just carrying no risk.
Wrong — no encryption is involved here at all; the problem is how far the data was aggregated.
quiz.hint: Privacy that prevents the good decision is its own kind of failure.

variant.q: You anonymise a delivery list so thoroughly that couriers can't tell which district to visit. Diagnosis?
choices: Over-stripped: the purpose can no longer be served
explain: Wrong — minimisation that erases the one thing couriers actually needed isn't correct, it's over-correction.
Correct — the district was the smallest shape that still let couriers do their job. Stripping past it broke the purpose.
